title: 12 Aug 2026 (Cairo)
des: Saudi Prometric paediatrics recall, Cairo test centre, 12 August 2026

questions.question: A child cannot stand suddenly after an upper respiratory infection. Examination is normal except for ataxia, and CT brain is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Post-infectious (often varicella) acute cerebellar ataxia gives sudden truncal ataxia with normal consciousness and imaging. It resolves over weeks.

questions.question: How should pain be assessed in a child?
questions.exp: Use a validated age-appropriate scale (FLACC, Wong-Baker faces, numerical scale).

questions.question: A child develops ataxia and loss of bladder control after a recent viral illness. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Post-infectious multifocal deficits suggest ADEM. MRI shows multifocal white-matter lesions.

questions.question: How much does length increase per month in the second 3 months of life?
questions.exp: Length grows about 3-4 cm/month in months 0-3, 2 cm/month in months 3-6 and 1-1.5 cm/month from 6-12 months.

questions.question: A toddler cries, then holds his breath, turns blue and briefly goes limp, then recovers fully. What is the management?
questions.exp: Breath-holding spells are benign. Check for iron deficiency, which makes them worse, and reassure.

questions.question: A child has focal seizures with eye blinking and a normal neurological examination. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Recurrent focal events need an EEG to define the epilepsy type.

questions.question: How are tics diagnosed?
questions.exp: Tics are diagnosed clinically.

questions.question: A 3-year-old with poor eye contact, no response to her name and repetitive play is assessed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Impaired social communication with restricted, repetitive behaviour is autism spectrum disorder. Check hearing as part of the work-up.

questions.question: A child has ataxia telangiectasia. What is the immune defect?
questions.exp: AT combines progressive ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia and immunodeficiency (low IgA, IgG2 and IgE). AFP is raised.
questions.d: Low IgA and IgG with recurrent infections

questions.question: A child has acute flaccid weakness of the legs with a sensory level and a positive Babinski sign. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Transverse myelitis needs MRI of the spine to show the cord lesion and exclude compression.

questions.question: A girl on medication for constipation has a UTI. Which imaging looks for renal scarring?
questions.exp: DMSA shows renal scars after pyelonephritis. Constipation predisposes to UTI.

questions.question: A child with gastroenteritis and dehydration develops haematuria and a flank mass. Urine has more than 10 RBCs. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Dehydration can cause renal vein thrombosis: haematuria, a palpable kidney and thrombocytopenia. Doppler ultrasound confirms it.
questions.d: Doppler ultrasound of the renal veins

questions.question: A child with gastroenteritis develops acute kidney injury. Which test helps tell prerenal failure from acute tubular necrosis?
questions.exp: FENa below 1% means prerenal failure; above 2% means intrinsic (ATN).

questions.question: A child with nephrotic syndrome on steroids for 6 months has membranoproliferative GN on biopsy. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Steroid-resistant MPGN is treated with immunosuppression; the recall keyed cyclophosphamide with pulsed steroids.

questions.question: A child with HUS has high creatinine and urea, high blood pressure and potassium of 8. What is the management?
questions.exp: Dangerous hyperkalaemia, fluid overload or uraemia in HUS are indications for dialysis.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia has septic arthritis. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: Salmonella is the classic cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis in SCD; Staphylococcus aureus is also common.

questions.question: A 20 kg child with haemophilia B needs a 50% rise in factor IX. What dose do you give?
questions.exp: Factor IX dose (IU) = weight (kg) × desired rise (%) × 1, so 20 × 50 = 1000 IU. For factor VIII the multiplier is 0.5.

questions.question: A child with haemophilia A was given factor VIII but did not improve. What is the next step?
questions.exp: A failure to correct suggests a factor VIII inhibitor. A mixing study (and Bethesda assay) shows it.

questions.question: A child has iron deficiency anaemia. Which result fits?
questions.exp: IDA is microcytic and hypochromic with low ferritin and high TIBC.
questions.a: Low Hb, MCV and MCHC with low ferritin

questions.question: A child's marrow shows 10% blast cells with dysplasia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Blasts under 20% with dysplasia is myelodysplastic syndrome; 20% or more is acute leukaemia.

questions.question: HbF is still 100% after 2 weeks of life (no HbA). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: No HbA at all means no beta chain production (beta-zero thalassaemia major).

questions.question: A child has a murmur with fixed splitting of the second heart sound. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Wide fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of ASD.

questions.question: A short child (115 cm) has an ejection systolic murmur. What is the lesion?
questions.exp: Short stature with supravalvular aortic stenosis is Williams syndrome.

questions.question: An infant with a large VSD is on all heart failure drugs but is not thriving. What is next?
questions.exp: Failure of maximal medical therapy (or pulmonary hypertension) is an indication for early surgical closure.
questions.a: Add another diuretic and wait a year

questions.question: A child is in stable SVT on the ECG. What do you give?
questions.exp: Adenosine is first-line after vagal manoeuvres in stable SVT.

questions.question: What arrhythmia is typical after an atrial switch operation for TGA?
questions.exp: Atrial (Mustard/Senning) switch scars the atria and causes sinus node dysfunction. Recalls key sick sinus syndrome for "ECG after TGA surgery".

questions.question: An infant has infantile spasms with an irregular EEG (hypsarrhythmia). What is the treatment of choice when tuberous sclerosis is the cause?
questions.exp: Vigabatrin is first line for infantile spasms with tuberous sclerosis. ACTH or prednisolone is used for other causes.

questions.question: A child has resistant seizures and hypopigmented skin patches. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ash-leaf macules with epilepsy suggest tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question: An infant has bilious vomiting but is haemodynamically stable. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilious vomiting in infancy is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

questions.question: An infant with bilious vomiting and suspected volvulus is stable. What is the management?
questions.exp: Resuscitate, refer to surgery and confirm with an urgent upper GI contrast study.
questions.b: IV fluids, surgical referral and upper GI contrast study

questions.question: What is most important in the first management of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.exp: Correct dehydration and hypochloraemic alkalosis before surgery.
questions.c: IV fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolytes

questions.question: A child has suspected appendicitis but the diagnosis is unclear. What is the most useful investigation?
questions.exp: Ultrasound is first line in children (no radiation). The recall writer chose CT abdomen; CT is used if ultrasound is not diagnostic.

questions.question: After a pull-through operation for Hirschsprung disease, a child has enterocolitis with bloody diarrhoea. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Hirschsprung enterocolitis is treated with rectal washouts, IV fluids and antibiotics.
questions.c: Rectal irrigation with warm saline and antibiotics

questions.question: A child with coeliac disease is on a gluten-free diet. Which test checks compliance?
questions.exp: Falling tTG IgA levels show adherence. Biopsy is not needed for monitoring.

questions.question: A child is brought for a check-up. All the family are thin, weight is on the 10th centile and growing parallel to it, and examination and tests are normal. What is the management?
questions.exp: A healthy child growing along a low centile with a similar family needs reassurance and growth monitoring.

questions.question: A picture shows bowel covered by a membrane protruding from the umbilicus. What is it?
questions.exp: Exomphalos is covered by a sac and often has other anomalies; gastroschisis is uncovered and to the right of the cord.

questions.question: A newborn with respiratory distress has a scaphoid abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A scaphoid abdomen with bowel in the chest is CDH.

questions.question: A picture shows an occipital skin-covered sac containing brain tissue. What is it?
questions.exp: An encephalocele contains brain tissue.

questions.question: A newborn is drooling with a soft abdomen and a coiled NG tube with no gas in the abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: No abdominal gas means no distal fistula.

questions.question: A child has recurrent pneumonia in the left lower lobe. What is the likely lesion?
questions.exp: Sequestration, usually in the left lower lobe with a systemic arterial supply, causes recurrent infection in the same place.
questions.c: Foreign body in the right bronchus

questions.question: A child with a history of migraine has an acute attack not helped by paracetamol. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Ibuprofen first; nasal sumatriptan is used in adolescents for acute attacks. Propranolol and topiramate prevent attacks.

questions.question: A child watches TV for long hours and eats junk food. What is the first step in management?
questions.exp: Lifestyle and behaviour change is the first step.

questions.question: Gratification (infantile masturbation) is diagnosed. What is the management?
questions.exp: It is benign and needs reassurance and distraction.

questions.question: A girl has short stature and a webbed neck. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Turner syndrome is confirmed by karyotype.

questions.question: An infant has hypotonia and tongue fasciculations. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: SMA is diagnosed by SMN1 deletion testing.

questions.question: Antenatal ultrasound showed multiple cysts in the chest. The baby is well after birth. What do you do?
questions.exp: CT chest characterises antenatally detected lung lesions.

questions.question: A child has bronchopneumonia that looks atypical. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Atypical (Mycoplasma) pneumonia in school-age children is treated with a macrolide.

questions.question: A 10-year-old has meningitis and cannot flex his neck. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Beyond the neonatal period, empirical treatment is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin where resistant pneumococci occur.

questions.question: An oncology patient on chemotherapy has a skin infection. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Infected neutropenic children need broad IV Gram-negative cover including Pseudomonas.

questions.question: A child with ALL has a central line and shock. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Line sepsis with shock needs Gram-negative and Gram-positive (MRSA) cover.

questions.question: A child with acute otitis media becomes irritable. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Irritability or seizures in a child with otitis media suggests meningitis, so do an LP.

questions.question: What is the treatment of acute otitis media?
questions.exp: High-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day) is first line.

questions.question: After treatment of otitis media there is still a middle ear effusion. What do you do?
questions.exp: Effusion after AOM usually clears; re-check in about 3 months.

questions.question: A child with pneumonia on treatment develops a large effusion. What is the management?
questions.exp: A large or infected parapneumonic effusion that does not respond needs drainage.

questions.question: A child on treatment for pneumonia develops a tympanic percussion note. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hyper-resonance means air in the pleura.

questions.question: An IV drug user develops infective endocarditis. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: S. aureus is the commonest organism in IV drug users. Viridans streptococci are commonest overall in children.

questions.question: A child has a mild viral illness without fever on the day of vaccination. What do you do?
questions.exp: Minor illness without fever is not a contraindication.

questions.question: A child on high-dose steroids has a cushingoid face. What about live vaccines?
questions.exp: High-dose steroids (≥2 mg/kg or ≥20 mg/day for 14 days or more) mean deferring live vaccines for at least a month after stopping.

questions.question: A child with ALL has a brother due for vaccines. Which vaccine should the brother not receive?
questions.exp: OPV virus is shed in stool and can infect an immunocompromised contact. MMR and varicella can be given to contacts.

questions.question: What are the dimensions of healthcare quality?
questions.exp: These are the six IOM dimensions of quality.
questions.c: Safe, effective, patient-centred, timely, efficient and equitable

questions.question: A laboratory result is given by phone. What should you do?
questions.exp: Verbal results must be written down and read back.
questions.c: Write it down and read it back to confirm

questions.question: During CPR, what is most important for the team leader?
questions.exp: The leader directs the team with closed-loop communication.

questions.question: Which pneumonia needs a follow-up chest X-ray?
questions.exp: Round pneumonia can mimic a mass, so a follow-up film confirms resolution.

questions.question: A child has a toxic appearance, drooling and stridor (epiglottitis). What is the initial airway management?
questions.exp: Keep the child calm and secure the airway in theatre with ENT and anaesthesia.
questions.a: Secure the airway by intubation in a controlled setting
questions.c: Examine the throat with a spatula

questions.question: A child snores at night with suspected obstructive sleep apnoea. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Polysomnography is the gold standard.

questions.question: A child on chemotherapy for ALL has multiple small liver lesions on ultrasound. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Bull's-eye liver lesions after neutropenia are typical of hepatosplenic candidiasis.

questions.question: A child with coeliac disease has itchy vesicles on the elbows (picture). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin form of coeliac disease.

questions.question: After a road traffic accident a child has a tender abdomen, anaemia and ongoing shock after fluids. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Ongoing haemorrhagic shock after 40 mL/kg crystalloid needs blood.

questions.question: A child has pancytopenia with low Hb, platelets and WBC (aplastic anaemia) and has a matched sibling. What is the definitive treatment?
questions.exp: HSCT from a matched sibling is curative for severe aplastic anaemia.

questions.question: A picture shows dark velvety skin on the neck. What does it indicate?
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans is a marker of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk.

questions.question: Cystic fibrosis is associated with which acid-base disturbance?
questions.exp: Salt loss in sweat causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (pseudo-Bartter).

questions.question: A child has a facial port-wine stain (Sturge-Weber syndrome). What should be screened for?
questions.exp: Glaucoma is a key complication; check eye pressures regularly.

questions.question: A child has polyuria, hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis and normal blood pressure. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bartter: hypokalaemic alkalosis, high renin and aldosterone, normal BP and hypercalciuria.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has respiratory distress, chest pain and hypoxia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: New infiltrate with chest pain, fever or hypoxia in SCD is acute chest syndrome.

questions.question: A child on chemotherapy has contact with chickenpox. What do you give?
questions.exp: VZIG for non-immune immunocompromised contacts.

questions.question: A boy has a long face and large ears. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Fragile X is diagnosed by FMR1 DNA testing.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of acute infectious diarrhoea in children in Saudi Arabia?
questions.exp: Rotavirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis in young children. The recall gave Salmonella, rotavirus, Shigella and E. coli as options; the writer's choice was not clear.

questions.question: How is dermatomyositis definitively diagnosed?
questions.exp: Muscle biopsy is definitive, though MRI and typical features often suffice; CK is the first test.

questions.question: What is an indication for admission in croup?
questions.exp: Stridor at rest, recession, hypoxia or cyanosis, or toxicity need admission.

questions.question: A brother and sister fight, each saying the mother loves the other more. What is the management?
questions.exp: Sibling rivalry is managed with behaviour advice.

questions.question: What is the classic feature of epidural haemorrhage?
questions.exp: Initial consciousness then deterioration (lucid interval) is classic for extradural haematoma.

questions.question: What is the empirical treatment of early neonatal sepsis?
questions.exp: Ampicillin (or benzylpenicillin) plus gentamicin covers GBS, E. coli and Listeria.

questions.question: A child with DKA deteriorates neurologically after initial stabilisation. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Treat suspected cerebral oedema with mannitol or hypertonic saline first, then image to exclude other causes.
questions.d: CT brain after starting treatment for cerebral oedema

questions.question: A child has a mild rash, fever and posterior auricular nodes (German measles). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: German measles is rubella.

questions.question: What is the most common site for an inhaled foreign body?
questions.exp: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.
